statement.title: Bank of England monetary policy statement, 18 June 2026
Bank of England monetary policy statement, 05 November 2026
paragraphs: At its meeting ending on 4 November 2026, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted by a majority of 8–1 to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%. One member voted to increase Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 4.25%.

The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month. Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level. UK CPI inflation increased to 3.5% in September. It is now expected to rise to around 5% by the middle of next year. It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation.

While the direct effects of higher energy prices are clear, and will continue to feed into firm and household energy bills, there remains limited evidence of knock-on effects on other prices and wages. However, the degree of inflationary pressure in the pipeline is now sufficient to warrant an increase in Bank Rate. Activity data in recent months have generally been stronger than expected, adding to the case for modestly tighter monetary policy.

Monetary policy is not on a pre-set path. The Committee will continue to assess the evidence at each meeting, in particular how likely high energy prices are to feed through to other prices and the economy more broadly, by monitoring the evolution of underlying pay, pricing behaviour, and slack. The Committee will adjust Bank Rate as necessary to ensure CPI inflation returns to the 2% target in the medium term.

The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month. Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level. UK CPI inflation increased to 3.5% in September. It is now expected to rise to around 5% by the middle of next year. It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation.

While the direct effects of higher energy prices are clear, and will continue to feed into firm and household energy bills, there remains limited evidence of knock-on effects on other prices and wages. However, the degree of inflationary pressure in the pipeline is now sufficient to warrant an increase in Bank Rate. Activity data in recent months have generally been stronger than expected, adding to the case for modestly tighter monetary policy.

Monetary policy is not on a pre-set path. The Committee will continue to assess the evidence at each meeting, in particular how likely high energy prices are to feed through to other prices and the economy more broadly, by monitoring the evolution of underlying pay, pricing behaviour, and slack. The Committee will adjust Bank Rate as necessary to ensure CPI inflation returns to the 2% target in the medium term.

Protracted conflict in the Middle East has contributed to further increases in crude and refined energy prices since the previous meeting, which remain more volatile and higher than pre-conflict. UK CPI inflation increased to 3.1% in August and is likely to rise further over coming quarters. Monetary policy is being set to ensure inflation comes down to 2% sustainably as the economy adjusts to the energy shock. The policy stance required to achieve this will depend on the scale and duration of the shock and how it propagates through the economy.

There has been little evidence so far of material second-round effects in price and wage-setting. However, the risk of such effects, against which policy needs to lean, is greater the longer higher energy prices persist or are more volatile. Activity has been slightly stronger than expected, although soft labour market conditions, and the higher interest rates faced by households and businesses since the conflict began, will act to reduce inflation over time. Overall, the Committee judges that the risks to the inflation outlook are tilted to the upside, and more so than at the time of the July Monetary Policy Report, although there remains scope for the outlook to change materially as events in the Middle East unfold.

The Committee judges that it is appropriate to maintain Bank Rate at this meeting. The Committee stands ready to act as necessary to ensure that CPI inflation remains on track to meet the 2% target in the medium term.

At this meeting, the MPC also voted unanimously to reduce the stock of UK government bond purchases held for monetary policy purposes, and financed by the issuance of central bank reserves, to zero. This will be conducted through a multi-year plan, such that the remaining stock is unwound at an annual average pace of £46 billion by the end of 2034, through annual sales of £20 billion alongside maturing gilts.

GBP:minutes:2026-06-18.label: Minutes
GBP:minutes:2026-06-18.title: Bank of England minutes of the 18 June 2026 meeting
points: Global energy prices had fallen but remained higher than pre-conflict, while UK two-year OIS rates were around 70 basis points above their pre-war level.
The Committee stated that CPI inflation was expected to be a little under 3% in 2026 Q3 and a little over 3¼% in Q4, after twelve-month CPI inflation had been 2.8% in May.

Members broadly agreed that a margin of slack had continued to emerge, while the Committee agreed it was too early to conclude one way or the other from the initial tentative and mixed evidence on second-round effects.

Members agreed that financial conditions had tightened materially since before the conflict, and most members judged that this tightening provided insurance against inflation risks while preserving optionality to adjust course.
The Committee maintained Bank Rate at 3.75% by seven votes to two, with two members preferring to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%.

points: The Committee said the Middle East conflict and its impact on energy prices and the UK economy remained the dominant uncertainty for the inflation outlook.
All members acknowledged sustained disinflation before the conflict, with abating domestic inflationary pressures supported by slowing wage growth and a soft labour market.
All members agreed that the likelihood of material second-round effects was the key uncertainty around the appropriate policy response to return inflation to target in the medium term.
The MPC judged that the risk of strong inflationary pressures was greater than the risk of weak inflationary pressures, with high uncertainty around the outlook.
Members said the appropriate policy stance involved current monetary policy restrictiveness and guarding pre-emptively against worse outcomes, while financial conditions had tightened materially.
Six members voted to maintain Bank Rate at 3.75%, while three voted against and preferred to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%.

points: The Committee reported CPI inflation of 3.1% in August and services inflation of 3.4%, while the Committee expected CPI inflation to reach slightly above 4% in 2027 Q1.
UK GDP had increased by 0.4% in 2026 Q2, and the Committee judged that there had likely been some stabilisation in slack.
UK financial conditions had tightened further since the July Report, and the quoted rate on two-year fixed-rate mortgages was around 95 basis points higher than prior to the conflict.

The Committee judged that risks to the inflation outlook were tilted further to the upside, while most members viewed UK short-term market interest-rate movements as imparting broadly sufficient monetary policy restraint.
Six members voted to maintain Bank Rate at 3.75%; three members voted against, preferring to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%.
The Committee unanimously voted to reduce the remaining stock of £368 billion of bonds to zero at an annual average pace of £46 billion by the end of 2034.

GBP:speech:7023fb334466.label: Speech
GBP:speech:7023fb334466.title: Financial resilience in an age of repeated shocks - speech by Andrew Bailey
points: Governor Bailey says lower growth, repeated supply shocks and changing market structures mean that resilience cannot be taken for granted.
Governor Bailey says potential growth is weaker in many economies, and central bankers should prepare for a world in which larger shocks are not rare exceptions.
Governor Bailey says a negative supply shock produces weaker output but higher inflation, while looking through a shock is possible only if inflation expectations remain well anchored.
Governor Bailey says strong banks and sound household and corporate balance sheets give policymakers room to respond without turning an economic adjustment into a financial crisis.
Governor Bailey says leveraged investors play a much larger role in government bond markets, and deleveraging in one market can spread quickly to others.
Governor Bailey says policy must raise sustainable growth, maintain credible policy frameworks, and ensure that financial markets can absorb shocks without amplifying them.

GBP:speech:7e1bc8c8f3d4.label: Speech
GBP:speech:7e1bc8c8f3d4.title: The low-gear labour market − speech by Clare Lombardelli
points: Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli says firms have adjusted much more by reducing demand for new workers than by shedding existing employees, and weaker hiring is by far the more significant driver of the unemployment rise.

Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli says the job-to-job switching rate has a pronounced downward trend, with more than 3% of employed people changing jobs each quarter thirty years ago and a little above 2% over the past year.

Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli says unemployment among 16 to 24-year-olds has risen much faster than for other age groups, and 16 to 24-year-olds account for more than half of the rise in aggregate unemployment since mid-2022.

Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli says that if jobseekers are not well matched to available vacancies, unemployment could remain higher for longer without producing the easing in wage pressure ordinarily expected.
Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli says business leaders expect AI to raise productivity meaningfully over the next few years, split broadly equally between increasing output and reducing employment.

Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli says the MPC voted by 8–1 to increase Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4%, and she continues to think there is likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term.

GBP:speech:8bd67b451c42.label: Speech
GBP:speech:8bd67b451c42.title: Physical shocks and economic resilience: a central bank perspective − speech by James Talbot
points: Physical Shocks And Economic Resilience says physical hazards can damage capital, reduce labour supply and productivity, disrupt transport and supply chains, and weaken demand and confidence.
Physical Shocks And Economic Resilience says central banks should focus closely on frequency, persistence and pass-through to overall inflation and inflation expectations.
Physical Shocks And Economic Resilience says the NGFS guide provides a five-step approach: identify, assess the propagation, assess whether a trade-off arises, set policy, communicate and monitor.

Physical Shocks And Economic Resilience says monetary policy cannot repair infrastructure, restore a harvest, or offset initial physical damage, and usually looks through short-lived first-round effects when expectations remain anchored.

Physical Shocks And Economic Resilience says fiscal space and insurance penetration help determine resilience, while repeated shocks can erode fiscal space, private-sector balance sheets and insurance capacity.

Physical Shocks And Economic Resilience says high insurance penetration and rapid payouts can reduce household distress, firm insolvency and credit losses while supporting a faster recovery in output.

fragments.text: They can damage capital. They can reduce labour supply and lower productivity. They can disrupt transport and supply chains.
They can weaken demand and confidence among economic agents, tighten credit conditions and raise uncertainty.
Central banks should therefore focus closely on frequency, persistence and pass-through to overall inflation and inflation expectations.
The report provides a five-step approach to assess these impacts: identify, assess the propagation, assess whether a trade-off arises, set policy, communicate and monitor.
Monetary policy cannot repair infrastructure, restore a harvest, or offset the initial physical damage.
If the shock is short-lived and expectations remain anchored, the standard monetary policy response is usually to look through the first-round effects
Fiscal space, insurance penetration, climate adaptation, infrastructure quality, financial-market depth and institutional capacity all help to determine a country’s resilience threshold.
Repeated shocks can gradually erode the very buffers that help economies absorb losses in the first place, including fiscal space, private-sector balance sheets and insurance capacity.
High insurance penetration and rapid payouts can reduce household distress, firm insolvency and credit losses as well as supporting a faster recovery in output.

quotes.text: Physical hazards can operate through several channels at once: They can damage capital. They can reduce labour supply and lower productivity. They can disrupt transport and supply chains.
The report provides a five-step approach to assess these impacts: identify, assess the propagation, assess whether a trade-off arises, set policy, communicate and monitor.
Monetary policy cannot repair infrastructure, restore a harvest, or offset the initial physical damage.
Repeated shocks can gradually erode the very buffers that help economies absorb losses in the first place, including fiscal space, private-sector balance sheets and insurance capacity.
High insurance penetration and rapid payouts can reduce household distress, firm insolvency and credit losses as well as supporting a faster recovery in output.

GBP:speech:cf08be27b6a5.label: Speech
GBP:speech:cf08be27b6a5.title: Financial conditions: what’s priced in? − speech by Catherine L. Mann
points: Catherine Mann says she voted in the last two meetings for a 25 basis point increase in Bank Rate.
Catherine Mann says the gap between the OIS curve and survey expectations widened further, implying over 100 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the coming 12 months.
Catherine Mann says a term structure model attributes around 24 basis points of the UK yield increase to higher term premia, compared with just 4 basis points in Germany.

Catherine Mann says monetary policy uncertainty increased significantly following the March decision and cannot simply be attributed to uncertainty around the economic outlook resulting from the conflict.
Catherine Mann says the Bank’s updated short-term inflation forecast from September projects inflation to increase to over 4% in Q1 2027.
Catherine Mann says real financial conditions are insufficiently tight and calls for a clearly communicated reaction function and a sufficiently restrictive path for Bank Rate.

fragments.text: I voted in the last two meetings for a 25 basis point increase in Bank Rate.
Since then, the gap has widened further, implying over 100 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the coming 12 months.
According to this term structure model, higher term premia account for around 24 basis points of the increase in the UK, compared with just 4 basis points in Germany.
monetary policy uncertainty increased significantly following the March decision, which cannot simply be attributed to uncertainty around the economic outlook resulting from the conflict.
the Bank’s updated short-term inflation forecast from September projects inflation to increase to over 4% in Q1 2027.
In my view, real financial conditions are insufficiently tight.

The appropriate response therefore is not to rely on risk premia to do the work of policy, but to reduce inflation risk and policy uncertainty through a clearly communicated reaction function and a sufficiently restrictive path for Bank Rate.

quotes.text: In my view, our current monetary policy stance is not sufficiently tight, which is why I voted in the last two meetings for a 25 basis point increase in Bank Rate.
Since then, the gap has widened further, implying over 100 basis points of tightening in Bank Rate over the coming 12 months.

I plot the estimated monetary policy uncertainty factor in the right panel of Chart 8, which shows that monetary policy uncertainty increased significantly following the March decision, which cannot simply be attributed to uncertainty around the economic outlook resulting from the conflict.
In my view, real financial conditions are insufficiently tight.

GBP:statement:2026-06-18.label: Statement
GBP:statement:2026-06-18.title: Bank of England monetary policy statement, 18 June 2026
points: The Monetary Policy Committee voted by a majority of 7–2 to maintain Bank Rate at 3.75%.
The Committee judges that, taking all the risks to the economic outlook into account, it is appropriate to maintain Bank Rate at this meeting.
CPI inflation has fallen to 2.8% since the previous meeting, although the Committee expects it to rise later this year as higher energy prices continue to pass through.
The Committee will continue to monitor closely the situation in the Middle East and how its impact propagates through the economy.
The Committee stands ready to act as necessary to ensure that CPI inflation remains on track to meet the 2% target in the medium term.
Two members voted to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%.

EXACT.label: EXACT
EXACT.help: Solved exactly from 1M month-average futures: the rate changes only on the effective date, so the implied rate after the meeting follows from the monthly average.

CURVE.label: CURVE
CURVE.help: OIS curve: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY and CHF use the Eurex Clearing settlement curves (discount factors), with the overnight rate fitted as constant between effective dates (one rate per interval); elsewhere an OIS forward curve averaged over the interval. Minus the overnight-to-policy spread.

ESTIMATE.label: ESTIMATE
ESTIMATE.help: No contract isolates this meeting: 1M/3M futures averages fitted with the rate changing only on effective dates and the smallest possible step changes. NZD also uses an estimated BKBM-OCR spread.

UPPER_BOUND.label: UPPER BOUND
UPPER_BOUND.help: 3M contract window: the average covers several meetings, so the cumulative move is an upper bound for this meeting alone.

PROXY.label: PROXY
PROXY.help: Government-curve proxy - not policy-equivalent. Shown as a raw sovereign level unless a basis can be measured from a short tenor.

DECIDED.label: DECIDED
DECIDED.help: The meeting has already been decided: it is part of the base rate.

level_help.bkbm: BKBM base: level of the ASX 90-day bank bill, not the OCR - no BKBM-OCR spread exists, so no bp vs the OCR
level_help.sovereign_proxy: sovereign proxy: raw government-curve level, not policy-equivalent

methodology.title: Base rate
methodology.text: The last rate DECIDED on or before the as-of date, including a decision that has been announced but is not in force yet (shown as 'from <date>'). The Fed is the midpoint of the target range.

methodology.title: Implied policy rate
methodology.text: Market instruments give the overnight benchmark path; the benchmark-to-policy spread (median of the last 20 business days, excluding +-2 business days around rate changes and month-ends) is removed to get a policy-equivalent rate.

methodology.title: Methods
methodology.text: EXACT: 1M month-average futures chain. CURVE: OIS curve - for USD (fed funds), EUR (EUR STR), GBP (SONIA), JPY (TONA) and CHF (SARON) the daily Eurex Clearing settlement curves: the overnight rate is taken as constant between effective dates and fitted to the published discount factors (least squares, one rate per interval, a small smoothing term only where pillars cannot separate two intervals), then the overnight-to-policy spread is removed (EFFR vs the Fed midpoint, EUR STR vs the deposit rate, SONIA vs Bank Rate, the call rate vs the BoJ guideline, SARON vs the SNB rate); a meeting whose effective date is beyond the last pillar is n/a. Otherwise an OIS forward curve averaged between effective dates. UPPER BOUND: 3M contracts whose window spans several meetings. PROXY: government curves / bills, with a basis measured only from tenors observed before the first effective date - without one ('proxy without short end') no bp, step or probability is computed and only the raw level is shown.

methodology.title: Estimates (ESTIMATE)
methodology.text: Where no contract isolates a meeting (CAD beyond the 1M CORRA chain, NZD bank bills), every 1M / 3M futures contract of the exchange is fitted at once: the overnight rate is constant between effective dates, each contract's average over its window equals 100 minus its price (days already past use the realised fixings), and among the paths that fit, the one with the smallest step changes is chosen. The step of an estimated meeting is its level minus the level of the previous point; a meeting no contract reaches is n/a and its move is inside the next one. No probability is computed for an estimate. NZD: bank bills are a BKBM level; the BKBM-OCR spread is an estimate (median of 3M interbank minus OCR over months without an OCR change around them), not a daily observation. If the actual BKBM-OCR spread is wider than assumed, every NZD point is lower by about the same number of bp.

methodology.title: Step and probability
methodology.text: For EXACT and CURVE the implied step at the next meeting is split into whole 25 bp moves (n = floor(|step|/25)) and a fraction p of one more: P(n+1 moves) = p, P(n moves) = 1 - p, in the direction of the step.

methodology.title: Cumulative bp
methodology.text: Implied policy rate after the last meeting of the year minus the base rate, in bp. Positive = hawkish.

methodology.title: Repricing
methodology.text: Change of the implied level at a fixed horizon (last meeting of 2026 / 2027) over 5 business days (1w) and 21 business days (1m); independent of decisions taken in between. The change of the cumulative bp is a secondary field.

methodology.title: GAP
methodology.text: Market minus bank, in bp: the Fed's median dot vs the implied rate at the last meeting of each year. Only where both are on the same basis.

methodology.title: Surprises and reaction
methodology.text: Surprise vs consensus: decided rate minus consensus. Surprise vs market: decided step minus the step implied at T-1 (EXACT / CURVE / PROXY with a basis only). Reaction: change of the implied level between the close of T-1 and T at the next meeting and at the last meeting of the year.

methodology.title: Pairs
methodology.text: Base minus quote, metric by metric: the current rate differential (carry), the implied differential at year end (both legs policy-equivalent) and its repricing (both legs need a change of level). The flag is the weaker of the two legs.

latency.title: Time from decision to site
latency.text: First seen = the moment the collector stored the statement; official time = the decision time in the bank's zone (the BoJ announces at a variable time: its own RSS timestamp). Target: within 15 minutes. An external trigger starts the collector at the decision; before it existed the statements were found by the regular runs.
